subproblems.title: Finite net from a maximal disjoint family of closed balls (packing count)
subproblems.statement: Let X be a metric space whose sigma-algebra contains all open sets (so closed balls are measurable), and let mu be a measure on X. Let S, E be subsets of X and r, a, b real numbers with r > 0, a > 0, b >= 0 and mu(E) <= b. Assume that for every y in S the closed ball B_r(y) = {x : dist(x,y) <= r} is contained in E and mu(B_r(y)) >= a. Then there is a finite set F contained in S with (#F) * a <= b such that every y in S satisfies dist(y, z) <= 2r for some z in F.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type) [MetricSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] [OpensMeasurableSpace X] (μ : Measure X) (S E : Set X) (r a b : ℝ), 0 < r → 0 < a → 0 ≤ b → μ E ≤ ENNReal.ofReal b → (∀ y ∈ S, closedBall y r ⊆ E ∧ ENNReal.ofReal a ≤ μ (closedBall y r)) → ∃ F : Finset X, (↑F : Set X) ⊆ S ∧ (F.card : ℝ) * a ≤ b ∧ ∀ y ∈ S, ∃ z ∈ F, dist y z ≤ 2 * r
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 5, printed proof of Lemma 2.5 (p. 109):
- "Recall the general principle that if K is compact and tau > 0 then any maximal pairwise disjoint collection B_{tau/2}(y_j) with y_j in K will automatically have the property that K is contained in the union of the B_tau(y_j)";
- together with the counting estimate (3): "C^{-1} N delta^{alpha n} <= sum_j mu(B_{delta^alpha/2}(y_j)) = mu(union_j B_{delta^alpha/2}(y_j)) <= mu(B_2(0)) <= 2C".
This is Step 4 of the parent proof (an admissible set of maximal cardinality), stated abstractly:
- centre set S (parent: spt V cap B_sigma(xi));
- radius r = tau/2 (parent: A sigma/2);
- container E (parent: B_{2 sigma}(xi));
- lower mass bound a (parent: (1/2) omega_n (A sigma/2)^n);
- upper bound b (parent: 2 omega_n (2 sigma)^n).
Compactness of K is not needed, because finiteness comes from the mass bounds. No erratum affects this step.

Hypotheses and notation.
- X is a metric space whose sigma-algebra contains the open sets, and mu is a measure on X with values in [0, infinity].
- B_t(y) := {x in X : dist(x, y) <= t} is the closed ball.
- S, E are subsets of X; r > 0, a > 0, b >= 0; mu(E) <= b in [0, infinity].
- For every y in S: B_r(y) is contained in E and mu(B_r(y)) >= a.

1. Measurability of balls. Each closed ball B_r(z) is a closed set. Its complement is open, hence measurable, so B_r(z) is measurable.

2. Admissible sets. Call a finite set G of points of X admissible if G is contained in S and the closed balls B_r(z), z in G, are pairwise disjoint, i.e. B_r(z) cap B_r(z') is empty whenever z, z' in G and z != z'. The empty set is admissible (vacuously).

3. Packing bound: every admissible G satisfies (#G) a <= b.
 (a) The sets B_r(z), z in G, are measurable (Step 1) and pairwise disjoint, so by finite additivity mu(union_{z in G} B_r(z)) = sum_{z in G} mu(B_r(z)).
 (b) Each z in G lies in S, so mu(B_r(z)) >= a, and the sum is >= sum_{z in G} a = (#G) a.
 (c) Each B_r(z) is contained in E (z in S), so the union is contained in E, and by monotonicity mu(union_{z in G} B_r(z)) <= mu(E) <= b.
 (d) Hence (#G) a <= b in [0, infinity]. Both (#G) a and b are nonnegative real numbers, so the inequality also holds in R.
 (e) As a > 0, #G <= b/a, and therefore #G <= floor(b/a).

4. A maximal admissible set. Let Cset := {#G : G admissible}, a set of natural numbers. By Steps 2 and 3, 0 is in Cset and every element of Cset is <= floor(b/a). A nonempty set of natural numbers that is bounded above contains its supremum N := sup Cset. Fix an admissible F with #F = N; then #G <= N for every admissible G.

5. First two conclusions. F is contained in S because F is admissible, and (#F) a <= b by Step 3.

6. Net property. Let y in S and suppose, for contradiction, that dist(y, z) > 2r for every z in F.
 (a) y is not in F: otherwise taking z = y would give 0 = dist(y, y) > 2r > 0.
 (b) For every z in F, B_r(y) cap B_r(z) is empty: if w belonged to both balls, then dist(y, z) <= dist(y, w) + dist(w, z) <= r + r = 2r, contradicting dist(y, z) > 2r.
 (c) G' := F union {y} is admissible: G' is contained in S because F is contained in S and y in S. Balls centred at two distinct points of F are disjoint because F is admissible, and the ball centred at y is disjoint from the ball centred at any z in F by (b).
 (d) By (a), #G' = #F + 1 = N + 1 > N, contradicting the maximality in Step 4.
 Hence some z in F satisfies dist(y, z) <= 2r.

7. Conclusion. By Steps 5 and 6, F is a finite subset of S with (#F) a <= b, and every y in S has dist(y, z) <= 2r for some z in F. QED

(Mathlib names for the steps: measurableSet_closedBall, measure_biUnion_finset, measure_mono, ENNReal.ofReal_mul, ENNReal.ofReal_natCast, ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal_iff, Nat.le_floor, le_div_iff₀, Nat.sSup_mem, le_csSup, Set.PairwiseDisjoint.insert, Metric.closedBall_disjoint_closedBall, Finset.card_insert_of_notMem.)
proof_key_steps: Admissible sets: finite G contained in S whose closed r-balls are pairwise disjoint; the empty set is admissible.
Packing count: (#G) a <= sum mu(B_r(z)) = mu(union B_r(z)) <= mu(E) <= b by finite additivity and B_r(z) contained in E; hence #G <= floor(b/a).
Choose an admissible F of maximal cardinality N (a nonempty, bounded-above set of naturals contains its supremum).

If y in S had dist(y,z) > 2r for all z in F, then y is not in F and B_r(y) is disjoint from every B_r(z), so F union {y} would be admissible of size N+1, a contradiction; hence every y in S is within 2r of F.

subproblems.title: Normal-part integral bounded by the conical-excess integrand (book (1))
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, mu a measure on R^(n+l), P : R^(n+l) -> L(R^(n+l), R^(n+l)) an arbitrary map into continuous linear endomorphisms, y in R^(n+l) and s > 0. Then the Lebesgue integral of ofReal(|(x - y) - P(x)(x - y)|^2) over the closed ball B_s(y) is at most ofReal(s^(n+2)) times the Lebesgue integral of ofReal(|(x - y) - P(x)(x - y)|^2 / |x - y|^(n+2)) over B_s(y). Here the quotient is 0 at x = y (real division by 0 is 0), ofReal(t) = max(t, 0), integrals take values in [0, infinity], and no measurability is assumed.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (P : Amb n ℓ → Amb n ℓ →L[ℝ] Amb n ℓ) (y : Amb n ℓ) (s : ℝ), 0 < s → ∫⁻ x in closedBall y s, ENNReal.ofReal (‖(x - y) - P x (x - y)‖ ^ 2) ∂μ ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (s ^ (n + 2)) * ∫⁻ x in closedBall y s, ENNReal.ofReal (‖(x - y) - P x (x - y)‖ ^ 2 / ‖x - y‖ ^ (n + 2)) ∂μ
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 5, printed proof of Lemma 2.5 (p. 109), inequality (1), first inequality (after rescaling to sigma = 1):
 int_{B_2(y)} |p_{(T_x M)^perp}(x - y)|^2 dmu <= 2^{n+2} int_{B_2(y)} |p_{(T_x M)^perp}(x - y)|^2 |x - y|^{-n-2} dmu.
This is Step 3 of the parent proof: "For x in B_{2 sigma}(y) with x != y, |p_x^perp(x - y)|^2 = |x - y|^(n+2) g_y(x) <= (2 sigma)^(n+2) g_y(x), and both sides vanish at x = y". Here it is stated for an arbitrary measure mu, an arbitrary map P in place of x -> p_x = V.tangentProj x, and an arbitrary radius s > 0 (parent: s = 2 sigma). No erratum affects this step.

Hypotheses and notation.
- n, l are natural numbers; mu is a measure on R^(n+l); for each x, P(x) is a continuous linear map R^(n+l) -> R^(n+l); y in R^(n+l); s > 0; B_s(y) is the closed ball.
- For real t, ofReal(t) := max(t, 0) in [0, infinity).
- Integrals are Lebesgue integrals over B_s(y) of [0, infinity]-valued functions (lower integrals; no measurability is assumed). Real division by 0 equals 0.
- Put v(x) := (x - y) - P(x)(x - y) and q(x) := |v(x)|^2 / |x - y|^(n+2). Thus q(x) >= 0 for all x, and q(y) = 0.

1. Pointwise inequality: for every x in B_s(y), |v(x)|^2 <= s^(n+2) q(x).
 (a) If x = y: then x - y = 0 and P(y)(0) = 0 by linearity, so v(y) = 0 and |v(y)|^2 = 0 <= s^(n+2) q(y), since s^(n+2) > 0 and q(y) >= 0.
 (b) If x != y: d := |x - y| satisfies 0 < d <= s because x in B_s(y). Then d^(n+2) > 0, so |v(x)|^2 = d^(n+2) (|v(x)|^2 / d^(n+2)) = d^(n+2) q(x). Since 0 <= d <= s and t -> t^(n+2) is monotone on [0, infinity), d^(n+2) <= s^(n+2). Multiplying by q(x) >= 0 gives |v(x)|^2 <= s^(n+2) q(x).

2. Passing to [0, infinity]. ofReal is monotone, and since s^(n+2) >= 0 we have ofReal(s^(n+2) q(x)) = ofReal(s^(n+2)) ofReal(q(x)). Hence ofReal(|v(x)|^2) <= ofReal(s^(n+2)) ofReal(q(x)) for every x in B_s(y).

3. Integration. B_s(y) is closed, hence Borel measurable. For [0, infinity]-valued functions f <= g at every point of a measurable set B (no measurability of f, g needed), int_B f dmu <= int_B g dmu. Therefore
 int_{B_s(y)} ofReal(|v|^2) dmu <= int_{B_s(y)} ofReal(s^(n+2)) ofReal(q) dmu.

4. Constant factor. c := ofReal(s^(n+2)) is finite, and for a finite constant c, int_B c g dmu = c int_B g dmu for every [0, infinity]-valued g (no measurability needed). Hence the right side of Step 3 equals ofReal(s^(n+2)) int_{B_s(y)} ofReal(q) dmu.

5. Conclusion. Combining Steps 3 and 4:
 int_{B_s(y)} ofReal(|(x - y) - P(x)(x - y)|^2) dmu(x) <= ofReal(s^(n+2)) int_{B_s(y)} ofReal(|(x - y) - P(x)(x - y)|^2 / |x - y|^(n+2)) dmu(x). QED

proof_key_steps: At x = y both integrands vanish: v(y) = 0 by linearity of P(y), and q(y) = 0 by the a/0 = 0 convention.
ofReal is monotone and ofReal(s^(n+2) q) = ofReal(s^(n+2)) ofReal(q) since s^(n+2) >= 0.
Integrate over the measurable closed ball (pointwise monotonicity, no measurability needed) and pull out the finite constant ofReal(s^(n+2)).

subproblems.title: Chebyshev selection of a point with an n-plane tangent and small normal parts (book (4)-(5))
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, mu a measure on R^(n+l), and P : R^(n+l) -> L(R^(n+l), R^(n+l)) mu-a.e. strongly measurable. Assume (A): for mu-a.e. x there is an n-dimensional linear subspace T with P(x) = p_T (the orthogonal projection onto T, T.starProjection). Let xi in R^(n+l), let s, R, K, lambda be real with lambda > 0 and s <= R, and let F be a finite subset of R^(n+l). Assume (H1): for each y in F, the Lebesgue integral of ofReal(|(x - y) - P(x)(x - y)|^2) over the closed ball B_R(xi) is <= ofReal(K). Assume (H2): ofReal((#F) K) < ofReal(lambda) mu(B_s(xi)) in [0, infinity]. Then there are x_0 in the closed ball B_s(xi) and an n-dimensional linear subspace T with P(x_0) = p_T and |(x_0 - y) - p_T(x_0 - y)|^2 < lambda for every y in F.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (P : Amb n ℓ → Amb n ℓ →L[ℝ] Amb n ℓ), AEStronglyMeasurable P μ → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, ∃ T : Submodule ℝ (Amb n ℓ), Module.finrank ℝ T = n ∧ P x = T.starProjection) → ∀ (ξ : Amb n ℓ) (s R K lam : ℝ) (F : Finset (Amb n ℓ)), 0 < lam → s ≤ R → (∀ y ∈ F, ∫⁻ x in closedBall ξ R, ENNReal.ofReal (‖(x - y) - P x (x - y)‖ ^ 2) ∂μ ≤ ENNReal.ofReal K) → ENNReal.ofReal ((F.card : ℝ) * K) < ENNReal.ofReal lam * μ (closedBall ξ s) → ∃ x₀ ∈ closedBall ξ s, ∃ T : Submodule ℝ (Amb n ℓ), Module.finrank ℝ T = n ∧ P x₀ = T.starProjection ∧ ∀ y ∈ F, ‖(x₀ - y) - T.starProjection (x₀ - y)‖ ^ 2 < lam
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 5, printed proof of Lemma 2.5 (p. 109), (4)-(5): "Thus for any given k >= 1 we have sum_{j=1}^N |p_{(T_x M)^perp}(x - y_j)|^2 <= C k delta^{1 - alpha n} except possibly for a set of x in B_1(0) cap spt mu of mu-measure <= 1/k. Since mu(B_{delta^alpha}(0)) >= C^{-1} delta^{alpha n} by 2.4, we can select k = C delta^{-alpha n}, thus ensuring that (4) holds for some x_0 in spt mu cap B_{delta^alpha}(0)".
This follows the explicit form of Step 5 of the parent proof: f := sum_j |p_x^perp(x - y_j)|^2, Chebyshev's inequality, positivity of the measure of the good set, and the choice of a point where p_x is the projection onto an n-dimensional T (aal_tangent_structure (a),(b)).
Here mu, P, the radii (parent: R = sigma, s = A sigma), the per-point bound K (parent: (2 sigma)^(n+2) C_P omega_n delta) and lambda (parent: (4 C_5/omega_n) delta^(1 - 2 alpha n) sigma^2) are arbitrary, and the parent's numerical estimate is packaged into hypothesis (H2). No erratum affects this step.

Hypotheses and notation.
- n, l are natural numbers; mu is a measure on R^(n+l); P : R^(n+l) -> L(R^(n+l), R^(n+l)) is mu-a.e. strongly measurable.
- (A) For mu-a.e. x there is a linear subspace T of dimension n with P(x) = p_T, where p_T := T.starProjection is the orthogonal projection onto T.
- xi in R^(n+l); s, R, K, lambda are real with lambda > 0 and s <= R; F is a finite subset of R^(n+l).
- (H1) For every y in F: int_{B_R(xi)} ofReal(|(x - y) - P(x)(x - y)|^2) dmu(x) <= ofReal(K).
- (H2) ofReal((#F) K) < ofReal(lambda) mu(B_s(xi)).
- Balls are closed; integrals are Lebesgue integrals in [0, infinity]; ofReal(t) = max(t, 0).

1. Notation. For y in F put h_y(x) := ofReal(|(x - y) - P(x)(x - y)|^2) and f(x) := sum_{y in F} h_y(x) in [0, infinity]. Let B := B_R(xi) and B' := B_s(xi). Both are closed, hence measurable, and B' is contained in B because s <= R.

2. Measurability of h_y.
 (a) The evaluation map (L, v) -> L(v), from L(R^(n+l), R^(n+l)) x R^(n+l) to R^(n+l), is continuous bilinear.
 (b) P is mu-a.e. strongly measurable and x -> x - y is continuous, so x -> P(x)(x - y) is mu-a.e. strongly measurable (Mathlib ContinuousLinearMap.aestronglyMeasurable_comp₂ applied to the identity map of L(R^(n+l), R^(n+l))).
 (c) Then x -> (x - y) - P(x)(x - y), its norm, the square and ofReal are mu-a.e. measurable. So h_y is mu-a.e. measurable, and also a.e. measurable for mu restricted to B.

3. Integral of f over B. By additivity of the Lebesgue integral for finitely many a.e.-measurable [0, infinity]-valued functions (Mathlib lintegral_finsetSum') and (H1):
 int_B f dmu = sum_{y in F} int_B h_y dmu <= sum_{y in F} ofReal(K) = (#F) ofReal(K) = ofReal((#F) K).
 The last equality holds because #F >= 0 gives ofReal((#F) K) = ofReal(#F) ofReal(K), and ofReal(#F) = #F.

4. Assumption for contradiction. Suppose the conclusion fails: for every x in B' and every n-dimensional subspace T with P(x) = p_T, there is y in F with |(x - y) - p_T(x - y)|^2 >= lambda.

5. Then f >= ofReal(lambda) a.e. on B', i.e. for a.e. x with respect to mu restricted to B'.
 (a) By (A) there is a mu-null set Z such that for every x outside Z some n-dimensional T_x satisfies P(x) = p_{T_x}. Z is also null for mu restricted to B', and almost every point for mu restricted to B' lies in B'.
 (b) For x in B' minus Z, Step 4 applied to (x, T_x) gives y in F with |(x - y) - P(x)(x - y)|^2 = |(x - y) - p_{T_x}(x - y)|^2 >= lambda.
 (c) So ofReal(lambda) <= h_y(x) <= f(x), because all summands of f are >= 0.

6. Chebyshev's inequality in the form needed:
 ofReal(lambda) mu(B') = int_{B'} ofReal(lambda) dmu <= int_{B'} f dmu <= int_B f dmu <= ofReal((#F) K).
 The four relations use, in order: the integral of a constant over B', a.e. monotonicity of the integral (Step 5), monotonicity in the domain (B' contained in B), and Step 3. This contradicts (H2).
 Equivalently: {x in B' : f(x) >= lambda} has mu-measure at most lambda^{-1} int_B f dmu < mu(B'). So Y = {x in B' : f(x) < lambda} has positive measure and, by (A), contains a point x_0 at which P(x_0) is the projection onto an n-dimensional subspace.

7. Conclusion. There exist x_0 in B_s(xi) and an n-dimensional subspace T with P(x_0) = p_T and |(x_0 - y) - p_T(x_0 - y)|^2 < lambda for every y in F. QED

If no good point existed, then by the a.e. n-plane hypothesis f >= lambda a.e. on B_s(xi).
Then lambda mu(B_s(xi)) <= int_{B_s(xi)} f <= int_{B_R(xi)} f <= (#F) K contradicts (H2); hence x_0 in B_s(xi) and T with P(x_0) = p_T and all |p_T^perp(x_0 - y)|^2 < lambda exist.

subproblems.title: Height bound from a net and a plane close to the net points (book (5)-(6))
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, T a linear subspace of R^(n+l) with orthogonal projection p_T (T.starProjection), xi, x_0 in R^(n+l), S a subset of R^(n+l), F a finite subset of R^(n+l), and a, b real numbers. Assume |x_0 - xi| <= a, assume |(x_0 - y) - p_T(x_0 - y)| <= b for every y in F, and assume every x in S has some y in F with dist(x, y) <= a. Then dist(x - xi, T) = inf{|x - xi - t| : t in T} <= b + 2a for every x in S.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (T : Submodule ℝ (Amb n ℓ)) (ξ x₀ : Amb n ℓ) (S : Set (Amb n ℓ)) (F : Finset (Amb n ℓ)) (a b : ℝ), ‖x₀ - ξ‖ ≤ a → (∀ y ∈ F, ‖(x₀ - y) - T.starProjection (x₀ - y)‖ ≤ b) → (∀ x ∈ S, ∃ y ∈ F, dist x y ≤ a) → ∀ x ∈ S, infDist (x - ξ) (T : Set (Amb n ℓ)) ≤ b + 2 * a
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 5, printed proof of Lemma 2.5 (pp. 109-110), (5)-(6) and the conclusion: "|p_{(T_{x_0} M)^perp}(y_j - x_0)| <= C delta^{1/2 - alpha n}; since |x_0| < delta^alpha, |p_{(T_{x_0} M)^perp}(y_j)| <= C(delta^{1/2 - alpha n} + delta^alpha) ... all the points y_1, ..., y_N are in the C delta^{1/(2n+2)} neighborhood of the subspace T_0 = T_{x_0} M, and hence by (2) we have dist(y, T_0) <= C delta^{1/(2n+2)} for all y in spt mu cap B_1(0)".
This is Steps 6-7 of the parent proof: the net points y_j (parent: F, an A sigma-net of spt V cap B_sigma(xi)), the selected point x_0, the plane T, a = A sigma = delta^alpha sigma and b = C_6 delta^alpha sigma, with the two triangle inequalities combined into one. No erratum affects this step.

Hypotheses and notation.
- n, l are natural numbers; T is a linear subspace of R^(n+l); p_T := T.starProjection is the orthogonal projection onto T, so p_T(v) is in T for every v.
- xi, x_0 in R^(n+l); S is a subset of R^(n+l); F is a finite subset of R^(n+l); a, b are real numbers.
- (i) |x_0 - xi| <= a.
- (ii) |(x_0 - y) - p_T(x_0 - y)| <= b for every y in F.
- (iii) For every x in S there is y in F with dist(x, y) = |x - y| <= a.
- For v in R^(n+l), dist(v, T) := inf{|v - t| : t in T} (Metric.infDist).

1. Fix x in S. By (iii) choose y in F with |x - y| <= a.

2. Put u := x_0 - y and t := -p_T(u). Since p_T(u) is in T and T is a linear subspace (closed under negation), t is in T.

3. Algebraic identity: (x - xi) - t = (x - xi) + p_T(u) = (x - y) + (x_0 - xi) - (u - p_T(u)). This holds because (x - y) + (x_0 - xi) - (x_0 - y) = x - xi.

4. Since t is in T, dist(x - xi, T) <= |(x - xi) - t|, because an infimum is at most each of its values.

5. By Step 3 and the triangle inequality,
 |(x - xi) - t| <= |x - y| + |x_0 - xi| + |u - p_T(u)| <= a + a + b,
 using Step 1, (i), and (ii) for this y in F.

6. Hence dist(x - xi, T) <= b + 2a. As x in S was arbitrary, the inequality holds for every x in S. QED

Remark: u - p_T(u) = p_{T^perp}(x_0 - y), so Step 5 is the book's estimate |p_{T^perp}(x - xi)| <= |p_{T^perp}(x_0 - y)| + |x_0 - xi| + |x - y|.

(Mathlib: Submodule.starProjection_apply_mem, Submodule.neg_mem, Metric.infDist_le_dist_of_mem, dist_eq_norm, norm_sub_le, norm_add_le.)
proof_key_steps: For x in S pick y in F with |x - y| <= a.
dist(x - xi, T) <= |(x - xi) - t| <= a + a + b = b + 2a by the triangle inequality and the hypotheses.
